Merge pull request #1279 from shinycake/windows-device-lost

Stop Quill freezing on Windows when a GPU reset meets a window opening or closing

Let Windows open and close windows while recovering a lost GPU device

handle_gpu_device_lost held the window list's read lock across SendMessageW,
which waits for the UI thread, while open_window and close_one_window block
the UI thread in write() without pumping messages. A GPU reset, or a wake
with a lost device, that met a window opening or closing froze the app until
it was killed.

for_each_after_unlock now copies the handles out, drops the guard, then
sends. A window opened during the first round still gets the second, since
each round reads the list again, and a window destroyed after the copy only
makes SendMessageW fail, which could already happen because DestroyWindow
does not touch the list.

Both tests pass. Every other holder of the list runs on the UI thread or
makes only calls that do not wait for it.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Test the Windows device-loss sends off Windows, showing they hold the window list

The two loops that send WM_GPUI_GPU_DEVICE_LOST and
WM_GPUI_FORCE_UPDATE_WINDOW to every window move unchanged into a std-only
helper, so rustc --test can run the code the vsync thread runs on any host,
and CI's Linux job runs it. The tests state what must hold while a send
waits: a writer can take the list. This commit fails both on purpose.
try_write refuses during all three sends, which is what leaves the UI
thread in write() in open_window or close_one_window, unable to answer
SendMessageW.

Keep windows repainting when DWM reports a bad refresh period

On Windows the vsync thread starts by asking DWM for the refresh period. A
period under 1 ms fell back to the refresh rate through arithmetic that
divides by numerator / 1,000,000, so 60/1 or 60000/1001 divided by zero,
the thread ended, and no window got another frame. A QPC clock under 1 MHz
hit the same division on the first call.

refresh_interval is now total: both reports go through one checked
conversion, and the first between 1 ms and 100 ms wins, or the 60 Hz
default. The upper bound matters as much as the zero check, since any
large period used to be accepted and then slept on whenever DwmFlush
returned early. The QPC unwrap goes too; a failure takes the existing path
to the default.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 (1M context) <noreply@anthropic.com>

Test the Windows vsync interval off Windows, showing it divides by zero

The vsync thread's interval arithmetic moves unchanged out of vsync.rs into
a std-only module, so rustc --test can run the code the thread runs on any
host, and CI's Linux job runs it. The tests state what a bad DWM report
should give. This commit fails 13 of 14 on purpose: ten divide by zero, one
takes a 58,000 year sleep as the interval, one takes a zero sleep, and one
is 2% off on a 14.3 MHz clock.

Keep the chat list's animated emoji where they are when you switch chats (#1274)

Opening another chat in the main window let go of everything the main window used, chat list included. So every switch restarted the list's emoji statuses and custom emoji in previews from frame 0, even at rest. A row rebuilt before its reopened clip had a frame flashed its fallback (the star or the plain emoji).

A play head now belongs to a part of its window, Chat or Chrome, named by its caller (HeadId::of). A main-window chat switch lets go of the Chat part only; a closing chat window still lets go of everything. The chat you left still closes its clips and replays its once-stickers on return, including an empty chat's greeting and a business intro sticker. Chrome clips nothing shows close through the 5 s closer.

Mac: fallback flash on 0 of 50 clicks (main: 1 and 5), list emoji stay at rest with looping off, footprint right after 50 clicks 64 MB (main: 77-78 MB).

Decision record: docs/decisions/chat-switch-clips.md.

Keep a chat window's round videos and GIFs playing while the main window draws (#1269)

Inline players are tracked per window: passes, sweeps, on-demand requests, the GIF panel flag and paint marks. Before, the main window's passes aged a chat window's clips, which then reopened every frame: 95% CPU and 57 reopens a second for one round video, with the clip stuck on its placeholder. It is now 16% CPU and 0 reopens.

A clip no longer freezes when its window loses focus to another Quill window. The frame clock asks for frames while any Quill window is active (AppGate). The main and chat windows draw unfocused at a 30 ms interval instead of GPUI's 33.3 ms, which is exactly two 60 Hz vsyncs and let jitter push every other frame to 50 ms. An unfocused clip now draws 22-23 f/s, and everything animating draws 29 f/s per window.

A hidden window's clips pause and sleep after 2 s. A sleeping clip keeps its last picture until its reopened player has one, so restoring or uncovering main no longer flashes the green placeholder. That picture is retired again when it leaves.

The gate is recomputed when a chat window closes. A woken clip behind another app waits for its own window's pass. A click parked in a closed window is dropped.

Decision record: docs/decisions/inline-players-per-window.md.

Hotspot-change: the main window's activation observer in app_demo.rs hands the animation gate to QuillApp::follow_windows instead of setting it from the main window alone

Carrier host tests no longer fail at random or wait on the clock (#1273)

The carrier host tests wrote each stand-in helper script at run time and started it right away. A child that another test thread forked while the script was still open for writing kept that descriptor until its exec, so starting the script failed with ETXTBSY and the open came back Terminated. CI hit this three times in two days. The stand-ins are now checked-in scripts in tests/fixtures/carrier-helper.

a_held_generation_is_not_swept had the same descriptor sharing on a flock and now unlocks before dropping.

The tests no longer sleep, poll or assert on elapsed time:
- They wait on the host's channels. A wait whose report never comes ends when the carrier's threads do, at the latest at the start watchdog.
- The shutdown ceiling and close grace are fields, always SHUTDOWN_WAIT and CLOSE_GRACE outside tests. stop reports NotAtAll, UntilAllGone or GaveUp.
- The core test step in CI has a 30 minute timeout, so a hang fails instead of holding the job.

Production behavior is unchanged. The evidence and runs are in docs/decisions/carrier-helper-test-flake.md.

Write the headline by hand, then morph it into the headline font

The quill now writes the headline in Sacramento, a thin cursive (OFL,
subset and renamed Quill Hand), tracing every letter from stroke plans.
When the pen lifts off, a wave runs through the handwriting and each
letter's ink flows into its Inter Display letter.

The morph runs in WebGL 2. Each character gets a signed distance field
in both fonts, built in the page from the browser's own rendering of the
glyph. Per letter, the handwriting slides and stretches onto the typed
letter while the type swells out from the handwritten line and anything
outside it is cut back, joined with a smooth maximum. Without WebGL 2,
the ink crossfades into the text instead.

The pen keeps the slowed on-screen speed: 0.0285 em per ms of the
handwriting, which is set at 1.25 times the headline's size.

Keep a chat window's stickers playing when the main window switches chats (#1268)

* Keep a chat window's stickers playing when the main window switches chats

Every window draws stickers and custom emoji through one player. Opening
another chat in the main window (or moving its chat into a window of its
own) called stop_sticker_playback, which closed every clip, forgot every

chat open in its own window then showed each sticker and emoji as its
still and played it again from the first frame, and stickers set to play
once (looping off) and lone emoji that had rested played again.

The player now notes which windows use each clip and head. When a window
lets go of its chat, Player::leave forgets the heads only that window
drew and closes the clips only it asked for; what another window uses
stays as it is. QuillApp::leave_sticker_chat runs it and forgets the
left chat's lone emoji plays (EmojiPlays::leave_chat). The main window
calls it on a chat switch and when its chat moves to a window, so the
chat it left plays from the start next time, as in tdesktop, and its
clips close at once as before. A chat window calls it as it closes,
which also makes the chat play again when its window is opened again.
Stopping everything stays for an account switch, the loop setting and
the app going.

player module under the file-size limit.

A main window covered by its own chat window stops animating (#1264)

* A main window covered by its own chat window stops animating

With a chat open in its own window that covers the whole main window and
is active, the main window kept drawing its animated stickers and emoji:
89 to 104 frames a second on a 120 Hz Mac, about 20% of a core, and it
kept the spare drawables a stopped window gives back (about 14 MB).

The main window counted as active whenever any chat window was
(app_render), so its animation layers kept asking the frame clock for
ticks, and macOS never reports a window occluded by a titled window of
its own app. A chat window's own animated content also asked for
whole-app ticks, which redrew the main window under it at its rate.

Each chat window now notes its activation and place (bounds and display)
at its render and in its activation, bounds and display observers; the
main window notes its own at its render. While the active chat window's
bounds hold the main window's on the same display, the frame clock gives
the main window's slices and layers no tick, and a chat window's content
redraws only its own window. When the chat window moves, shrinks, goes
fullscreen or to another display, or is deactivated, the app redraws and
the main window animates again; closing it or activating the main window
already redraws. Fullscreen windows and Linux (no window positions on
Wayland, focus without raise on X11) never count as covering. The app's
own gate (frame.window_active) is unchanged, so the chat window's
animations, presence and notifications behave as before.

The test platform gained simulate_window_move and
simulate_window_move_to_display (gpui-pre, test support only).

* Keep a covered main window animating while Windows activates on hover

The covered check assumes the active window is in front of Quill's
other windows. With Windows' "Activate a window by hovering over it with
the mouse" on, the window under the pointer becomes active and may stay
behind, so an active chat window whose bounds hold the main window's
could sit under a visible main window, which would then hold still.

While SPI_GETACTIVEWINDOWTRACKING is on (or cannot be read), the main
window never counts as covered. The setting is read each time the check
runs, only once a chat window's bounds already hold the main window's:
at the main window's render and at each activation, move or resize of a
chat window, the events that could put an active chat window behind it.
No new crate feature: windows-sys Win32_UI_WindowsAndMessaging was
already on.

cover.rs and the decision doc list where the main window never counts as
covered (fullscreen, Linux, this Windows setting) and why macOS has no
such case today: Cmd-click and Cmd-drag reorder without activating but
need a visible part of the main window, Quill raises the main window only
with makeKeyAndOrderFront, and neither it nor a chat window is ever lifted
above the normal level.

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_016ibQTFUNwgzdGPax2ekg1E

* Keep call windows and chat window dialogs animating over a covered main window

While the active chat window covered the main window, the frame clock
dropped every whole-app tick asked with the main window's state in
place, and sent one asked in a chat window's scope to that chat window
alone. But any window's content asks for whole-app ticks, and the state
in place says nothing about which: the group call window's microphone
halo and speaking blobs ask with the main window's state in place (live
mode puts it back at every poll), and so do dialogs, sheets and toasts
in a chat window, which the kit builds after the window's view has put
back the state it found. They froze while the main window was covered,
or another chat window redrew in their place.

Now only the main window's own ticks (its slices and animation layers)
are dropped while it is covered, including those asked just before. A
whole-app tick runs as always and refreshes every window but the main
one, in place of the app notify that redraws them all. A chat window
that comes over the main window now marks it covered at once, so the
main window no longer draws one more frame first.

Tests: a call-like window and a ticking kit dialog in the covering
chat window draw as many frames as with the main window in view (both
drew 1 frame in 2 s instead of 60 before); the main window moved or
resized out from under the chat window animates, and within it does
not; and every resume is counted from the change itself, against the
main window coming back from behind another app, so a late start
fails. The decision doc also notes what inherently still shows a
covered main window still (Mission Control, App Expose, taskbar
previews, a screen share of the main window alone).

Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_016ibQTFUNwgzdGPax2ekg1E

* Redraw only the windows that follow the app while the main window is covered

While the active chat window covered the main window, a frame-clock tick
for the whole app refreshed every window but the main one. A refresh
also redrew windows that draw by their own clock and never followed the
app (Picture-in-Picture, notification popups), and rebuilt every cached
view, so the call window's pictures and the group stream picture were
built again on each tick.

Now the tick emits an AppTick event from QuillApp in place of its
notify, and only views that follow the app hear it: follow_app observes
the app and subscribes to AppTick, and the chat, call, group call,
stream, screen chooser and What's New views use it where they observed
the app before. Those redraw as on the notify; other windows and cached
views that do not follow the app keep their frame, as on the notify.

chat_window_placed now also asks the platform whether the main window
is the active one before marking it covered, so the answer does not
depend on which window's activation callback runs first.

A new test opens a call-like window with a cached picture and a window
that draws by its own clock: while the call window animates under a
covering chat window, the picture is not built again and the other
window draws nothing (60 builds and 60 frames in 2 s with the refresh).

Test the Opus FFT in CI and drop leftover decoder debug work

The vendored opus-decoder is not a workspace member, so its FFT tests only
ran by hand. kiss_fft.rs is std-only; scripts/test-opus-fft.sh builds it
alone with rustc --test, and CI runs it (5 tests, 0.1 s).

The decode test's music claimed transients but the encoder coded only one
transient frame across all six streams. Sharper, more frequent noise
bursts over a quieter chord now give 4 to 8 transient frames in each
20, 10 and 5 ms music stream, and a mono 10 ms music stream joins them.
The test still fails on opus-decoder 0.1.1 (1.05 steps) and passes here
(0.62 at most).

Leftover debug work no longer runs while decoding: two format! strings
for no-op loggers (intra-energy and stereo frames) are gated behind the
constant-false debug_packet flag, and five process-wide SeqCst counters
that only fed disabled traces are the constant usize::MAX, as upstream
did. Output is bit-identical on 24 streams; the release build had
already optimized the strings away, so CPU is unchanged.

The FFT module doc no longer says the forward transform scales by 1/N.

Play Opus voice notes with about 55 times less decoding CPU

On the owner's Mac a 48 kHz Opus file still cost 16 to 20% CPU at 1x,
against 5.5% for the same audio as WAV. opus-decoder 0.1.1 ran the CELT
inverse MDCT's 480-point complex transform as a direct DFT that called
f64 sin_cos for every term: 230,400 calls per 20 ms frame and channel,
98.8% of the instructions decoding a 64 kbit/s stream. crates.io has no
newer release; upstream's master branch already has a mixed-radix FFT.

The crate is now patched (third_party/opus-decoder, QUILL-CHANGES.md)
with upstream master's kiss_fft.rs and mdct.rs: a radix 4/2/3/5 FFT over
precomputed twiddles with buffers the MDCT keeps. Two leftover debug-log
appends that opened a file under /Users/tadeusz on every CELT frame are
removed too, as upstream did. The crate's license files come from the
upstream repository at the release commit, and THIRD_PARTY_LICENSES.md
is regenerated.

Decoding takes 3.1 instead of 174 ms per second of 64 kbit/s mono
speech, 6.3 instead of 428 for 128 kbit/s stereo music (Linux, release).
The output is not bit-identical but closer to libopus: the DFT's twiddles
carried the error of an f32 pi, and the 16-bit output moves by at most
one step (-90 dBFS) on 0 to 5.3% of samples. All 12 RFC 8251 vectors pass.
A new test decodes CELT streams of every frame size against rusty-opus's

Free a chat window's sticker frames while the main window is minimized or closed (#1267)

* Free a chat window's sticker frames while the main window is minimized or closed

With the main window minimized, a chat window playing animated stickers
grew Quill by about 25 MB a second without bound (1.4 GB after 50 s on a
Mac), the same with the main window closed, and with no window left open
the retired pictures' pixels stayed (657 MB).

Images Quill makes (sticker and video frames, blurred previews) wait in
image_budget's retired list until no frame can show them. Only the main
window's render swept that list, and it judged "no frame can show it" by
the main window's frame count. With the main window not drawing, nothing
swept, and its frozen count made every retired frame look visible.

The retired list and its sweep move to image_budget/retired.rs and no
longer depend on the main window drawing. A sweep runs between frames and
asks every open window what its latest frame can show: for the main
window, what it drew and what its cached slices replay, as of its last
frame however long ago; for every other window, its latest frame by
GPUI's frame count. A frame only shows images that existed when it was
done, so frames retired after it can go. Each main frame now gets that
bound as soon as it is done, not when the next main frame starts. A
closed window shows nothing, and with no window open everything retired
goes. Sweeps still run as the main window starts a frame, and also in a
task woken by a retirement, a chat window's frame or a window closing.

Co-Authored-By: Claude Opus 5.5 <noreply@anthropic.com>
Claude-Session: https://claude.ai/code/session_016ibQTFUNwgzdGPax2ekg1E

* Sweep only after real retirements, and test the sweep a chat window relies on

The sticker player hands retire_all an empty list for every frame it
fetches, and each call woke the sweeper task: any animation cost an extra
sweep after every frame, even when only the main window played it and its
own frames already swept. retire_all now wakes the task only when it was
handed an image.

The sweeper task armed its wake only once it first ran, so a retirement
between starting it and its first run woke nothing. It is armed when the
task starts now.

A new test goes through the real sweep: a chat window lets go of the
picture its frame on screen shows without drawing. The picture must stay
in its atlas through the main window's frames and leave once the chat
window draws without it. The earlier window tests still passed with a
sweep that read no window but the main one; this one fails then, and
with a constant frame count for other windows.

The decision record now says why call and video chat windows, which
replay cached views, are still safe, and that a window that stops
drawing keeps every retired picture that existed at its last frame (not
only what it painted) until it draws or closes, and why that is not
narrowed here.

Play audio at 1x without the speed stretcher's search (#1265)

* Play audio at 1x without the speed stretcher's search

Every voice note, song and (on Linux and Windows) video soundtrack runs
through the pitch-preserving stretcher. For each 20 ms block it scored
every position in a +-12 ms window (576 to 577 correlations at 48 kHz),
even when the natural continuation was in that window, where it always
wins: it counts as a perfect score and another position must beat it by
1e-4, more than f32 rounding allows. At 1x that is every block, which
cost about a quarter of a core on an M1 Pro for any playback.

Tempo::pick now returns the natural continuation unsearched when it is in
the window. Output is unchanged at every speed; 1x scores nothing, and
other speeds search only when the stretch has pulled the continuation
out of the window. The read-ahead stays as it was, because the input read
is the player's position and a video's audio clock, so pause points and
lip-sync do not move.

Tests compare every output sample, and the input read after each one,
with a verbatim copy of main's routine at 1x (with seeks and to the end),
at 0.5x to 2x, and across 1x/other/1x switches; and count that 1x scores
no positions. See docs/decisions/tempo-1x.md.

* Check every skipped stretcher search in tests instead of a frozen copy

Review of the 1x change: the tests compared the stretcher with a 234-line
verbatim copy of main's routine, which only proved main equal to itself
once and would rot as the stretcher changes. Under test, Tempo::pick now
runs the search on every block it skips (moved into best_match) and
asserts it picks the same position, so every test that plays through the
stretcher checks the change on every block. The new tests drive that
check over 48, 44.1 (now with a tone of whole-frame period), 16 and
96 kHz, the player's speeds, switches and seeks, and pin the read-ahead
(8,832 samples before the second block at 48 kHz stereo) so skipping it
fails.

The claim that skipping the search never changes a block is now scoped:
proven below about 83.7 kHz; at 176.4 and 192 kHz contrived input can
make main pick another position, a shift of at most 12 ms with no
audible seam. The 1x output is the input within f32 rounding, not bit
for bit.
